source.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
source.authors: Thomas Heap; Tim Lawson; Lucy Farnik; Laurence Aitchison

record.tranche_reason: The study uses different measurements and toy setups to test whether superposed structure appears in randomly initialized networks, and evaluates SAE feature metrics on trained and randomized transformers.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-model SAE sparsity comparisons and trained-versus-randomized SAE metrics. The detailed feature examples are qualitative illustrations, not separately measured results; values available only in plots are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on trained and randomized Pythia models (70M to 6.9B). Randomized and Step-0 models give auto-interpretability scores matching or exceeding trained ones. This is a specific result that SAE-recoverable, interpretable sparse latents (V4's indirect evidence) are not by themselves evidence of learned features in real LLMs, so V4 needs restating. The toy section uses synthetic superposed data and untrained random MLPs, so it does not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Also note: the authors say trained-model features are qualitatively more abstract, especially in later layers. They explicitly do not claim SAEs fail to capture learned features; they claim only that aggregate metrics cannot show this.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates SAE features and toy-data sparsity rather than reproducing the original Toy Models of Superposition method; toy inputs are based on Sharkey et al. and the experiments use SAE sparsity as a proxy for superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and layer affect the reported metrics; auto-interpretability generally increases with model size, and entropy trends differ across model variants and layers. The paper also reports sensitivity to training-token count and SAE hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs on outputs of untrained random MLPs reach high sparsity whether inputs are superposed or Gaussian. Random MLPs also improve the sparsity frontiers of GloVe and Gaussian inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomly initialized networks preserve or amplify apparent superposition (SAE-sparsifiability) regardless of the input distribution.

record.problems: The toy-model output evidence uses SAE sparsity and reconstruction as proxies rather than directly measuring feature geometry. The paper states it focuses on Pythia and RedPajama and does not claim coverage of all model architectures or datasets. Five-seed uncertainty plots are reported for Pythia-70m; many plotted comparisons have no stated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No results intentionally omitted. The paper's GloVe-vector and random-MLP comparisons are not included as claim-version rows because they do not directly measure one of the listed version statements.

untested.parts: All of V1. There are no trained toy networks and no feature geometry, near-orthogonality, or sparsity transition. The toy section uses synthetic data and untrained MLPs.
All of V2; no capacity or importance allocation measured.
All of V3. It only remarks that neurons in random networks may be polysemantic; nothing is measured.
Whether real models spread features across many neurons; neuron-level distribution is not measured.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not measured. The paper only argues that aggregate metrics can't certify computational relevance.

missing.what: Explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm and CE loss score for trained vs randomized SAEs. Random variants are close to trained; the control is far lower.
Per-latent entropy vs fuzz AUROC. Only trained latents include high-entropy, high-AUROC latents.
Robustness checks: 1B-token training, expansion factor 16-128, k 16/32, and Pythia-1b R=2 SAEs. Auto-interp stays similar across these.
GloVe and Pythia-embedding sparsity frontiers vs Gaussian controls. The gap is smaller than for toy data.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T5: the core result argues that SAE interpretability is weak evidence for V4 unless checked against a randomized baseline. V1 is dropped because the toy rows concern synthetic data and untrained MLPs. Most numeric rows are AUCs pooled across layers from figure legends, from 100 sampled latents per SAE, with no error bars except the five-seed plots for Pythia-70m. In every model size, the Step-0 variant exceeds the trained variant on both scores.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure feature-direction geometry, near-orthogonality, regular geometric arrangements, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
The discussion of incidental polysemanticity is background; no result tests other causes of polysemantic neurons.
Does not establish that SAE latents are computationally relevant model features, or measure how broadly features are distributed across ordinary model neurons.

relationships.condition: Trained Pythia models, SAE latents vs chance
relationships.reason: Trained-model SAE latents are explained above chance: fuzz 0.63-0.79 and detection 0.57-0.72, versus Gaussian-embedding controls at 0.44-0.54 (r5, r10, r15, r20, r25, r30, r35, r40, r45, r50; controls r9, r14, r19, r24, r29).
relationships.display_finding: SAE latents from trained models scored 0.63–0.79 on fuzzing and 0.57–0.72 on detection, above Gaussian-embedding controls at 0.44–0.54.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Trained Pythia models, SAE latents vs chance
source_check.reason: The figure legends substantiate above-chance explanation scores for sparse SAE latents in trained models. This supports the indirect existential claim, without establishing learned computational significance.

relationships.condition: Randomized and Step-0 baselines, Pythia-410m to 6.9b, plus Step-0 at all sizes
relationships.reason: Random and Step-0 models match or beat trained auto-interp scores, so SAE-recoverable interpretable latents are not specific to learned representations. Example: 6.9b fuzz is 0.79 trained vs 0.87-0.88 random (r15-r28, r40-r53, r8, r13, r33, r38). Only 70m/160m re-randomized models score lower (r6, r7, r11, r12).
relationships.display_finding: Randomized and step-0 models matched or beat trained-model auto-interp scores (for 6.9b, fuzzing scored 0.79 trained against 0.87–0.88 random), so interpretable latents are not specific to learned representations. Only the re-randomized 70m and 160m models scored lower.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Randomized and Step-0 baselines, Pythia-410m to 6.9b, plus Step-0 at all sizes
source_check.reason: Randomized and Step-0 models yield similar or higher scores, qualifying the specificity of this evidence. The reason's assertion that only 70M/160M rerandomized scores are lower is too absolute: 410M fuzzing excluding embeddings is 0.63 versus 0.65 trained, although the paper treats them as similar.

relationships.reason: Trained-model latents become less token-specific in later layers, while random-model latents stay concentrated on one or few tokens. This is a preliminary sign that trained SAE features differ (r55 vs r56-r58).
relationships.display_finding: Trained-model latents became less token-specific in later layers, while random-model latents stayed concentrated on one or a few tokens, a preliminary sign that trained SAE features differ.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Token entropy measures activation concentration across token IDs, providing preliminary evidence of abstractness differences. Alone it does not test either feature distribution across neurons or sparse-feature recoverability named by V4.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Trained Pythia models, SAE latents vs chance
labels.reason: The figure legends substantiate above-chance explanation scores for sparse SAE latents in trained models. This supports the indirect existential claim, without establishing learned computational significance.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Randomized and Step-0 baselines, Pythia-410m to 6.9b, plus Step-0 at all sizes
labels.reason: Randomized and Step-0 models yield similar or higher scores, qualifying the specificity of this evidence. The reason's assertion that only 70M/160M rerandomized scores are lower is too absolute: 410M fuzzing excluding embeddings is 0.63 versus 0.65 trained, although the paper treats them as similar.

labels.label: supports
labels.reason: Token entropy measures activation concentration across token IDs, providing preliminary evidence of abstractness differences. Alone it does not test either feature distribution across neurons or sparse-feature recoverability named by V4.

relation.reason: The study experimentally tests the specificity of V4's indirect evidence using trained, randomized, Step-0 and randomized-input models.

tranche.reason: Randomized-model controls specifically qualify the inference from aggregate SAE interpretation scores to recovered learned representations.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 27 January 2026; the stated ICLR 2025 review status is not substantiated by this text. Authors explicitly distinguish limitations of aggregate metrics from a claim that SAEs fail to recover learned features.
